subject: Pathology
summary: Chronic interstitial lung diseases are a group of restrictive disorders causing progressive fibrosis of the lung interstitium, leading to stiff lungs, dyspnea, and eventual respiratory failure.

sections.p: A chronic interstitial lung disease (CILD) is defined by diffuse, bilateral involvement of the lung interstitium with fibrosis lasting >3 months, confirmed by imaging and/or histology.
b: HRCT showing reticulation, traction bronchiectasis, or honeycombing
Lung biopsy (when needed) showing fibroblastic foci and collagen deposition

t.b: What pattern of lung involvement is present? → Identifies fibrosis, ground‑glass, and honeycomb; guides diagnosis and staging
What is the restrictive physiology? → Reduced FVC and TLC with normal or increased FEV1/FVC; quantifies severity

sections.p: Severity is graded by forced vital capacity (FVC) and diffusing capacity (DLCO) and by radiologic extent of fibrosis.
b: Mild: FVC ≥ 80% predicted, limited HRCT changes
Moderate: FVC 50‑79%, HRCT with traction bronchiectasis
Severe: FVC < 50% or DLCO < 40%, honeycombing present

sections.p: CILDs are categorized by known exposure, systemic disease, or idiopathic origin.
b: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) – most common in high‑income settings
Chronic hypersensitivity pneumonitis – bird or mold exposure
Connective‑tissue disease (e.g., rheumatoid arthritis, systemic sclerosis)
Occupational dusts (silica, asbestos)
Infections prevalent in low‑resource areas: untreated pulmonary TB, HIV‑related pneumonitis, post‑malaria lung injury

sections.p: Patients develop insidious dyspnea on exertion, dry cough, and progressive fatigue; clubbing may appear in advanced disease.
b: Exertional dyspnea worsening over months
Non‑productive cough
Digital clubbing in 30‑40% of cases

sections.p: A stepwise approach combines imaging, functional testing, and targeted labs to uncover cause and assess severity.
b: Baseline HRCT and PFTs
Serology for autoimmune disease (ANA, RF, anti‑Scl‑70)
TB testing (GeneXpert, sputum smear) in endemic regions

t.b: Is a systemic disease present? → Positive antibodies suggest connective‑tissue disease; directs immunosuppressive therapy
Is active tuberculosis contributing? → Detects Mycobacterium tuberculosis; positive result mandates anti‑TB therapy

sections.p: Complications arise from progressive fibrosis, hypoxemia, and vascular remodeling.
b: Rapid decline in FVC (>10% in 6 months)
Resting hypoxemia (SpO2 < 88%)
Development of pulmonary hypertension or cor pulmonale

sections.p: Treat underlying cause, slow fibrotic progression, and provide supportive care.
b: Antifibrotic agents (pirfenidone, nintedanib) for IPF – inhibit fibroblast activity
Immunosuppression (mycophenolate, azathioprine) for autoimmune ILD – reduce inflammation
Corticosteroids for acute hypersensitivity pneumonitis or infection‑related ILD – dampen immune response
Oxygen therapy for chronic hypoxemia – improves quality of life
Pulmonary rehabilitation – enhances exercise tolerance

sections.p: Regular monitoring detects progression and complications early.
b: PFTs every 3–6 months
HRCT annually or when clinical change occurs
Vaccinations (influenza, pneumococcal) to prevent infections
Smoking cessation and avoidance of occupational dust

sections.p: Several diseases mimic CILD on imaging or symptoms.
b: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease – obstructive pattern on PFTs
Pulmonary sarcoidosis – granulomatous nodules, often hilar lymphadenopathy
Bronchiectasis – dilated airways with productive cough

sections.p: Certain findings may appear normal despite significant disease.
b: Normal chest X‑ray early in disease – CT needed for detection
DLCO may be preserved in early fibrosis but drop sharply later
Serology can be negative in early connective‑tissue disease

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden worsening of breathlessness or new chest pain
Signs of right‑heart failure (edema, jugular venous distension)

faq.q: Why is HRCT preferred over a plain chest X‑ray?
faq.a: HRCT visualises fine interstitial patterns and early fibrosis that a plain film cannot detect.
No, they slow progression and improve survival but do not reverse established fibrosis.
In end‑stage disease with severe functional decline despite maximal medical therapy.

exam: Describe the HRCT patterns that differentiate idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis from hypersensitivity pneumonitis.
Explain how pulmonary function test results guide staging of chronic interstitial lung disease.
List three reversible causes of interstitial lung disease and the specific treatment for each.
